Environmental Ed Day 2 A Time For Stillness

Sep 15, 2010 • Janice Cotcher

Last week our instructor told us to be prepared to spend Monday morning outside “barring a blizzard”. Since our reading for that class included an article on the concept of slow pedagogy, I estimated that our activity would be along those lines. For those not familiar with the concept:

Our “slow pedagogy of place” highlights the importance of the body in an education with various environments—as those bodies are lived in and over times in natural spaces. A slow pedagogy, or ecopedagogy, allows us to pause or dwell in spaces for more than a fleeting moment and, therefore, encourages us to attach and receive meaning from that place…That is, for any pedagogy claiming responsiveness to the ecologically problematic human condition, there needs to be a shift in emphasis from focusing primarily on the “learning mind” to re-engaging the active, perceiving, and sensuous corporeality of the body with other bodies (human and more-than-human) in making-meaning in, about, and for the various environments and places in which those bodies interact and relate to nature.

  • Payne, P.G. and Wattchow, B., Phenomenological Deconstruction, Slow Pedagogy, and the Corporeal Turn in Wild Environmental/ Outdoor Education., Canadian Journal of Environmental Education, volume 14, 2009, 15.

Since part of slow pedagogy is to take time to explore and reflect on our surroundings, I decided to bring along my camera. One of the reasons I love taking pictures fits perfectly within the aforementioned philosophy. I love to take a moment to notice all my surroundings – the micro and the macro. I love to record how things really were (one reason why I prefer candid pictures).

The class met at Joe Farfard’s sculpture Mind’s Garden, where we first discussed our readings for the day. This might sound strange, but our task for the morning was to find a spot to be still for 40 minutes. I could see how this could be hard for some people. Some may think it is silly or a waste of time. Others may have difficulty sitting and “doing nothing” for that long. But is it really doing nothing? How often do we get the opportunity to collect our thoughts? How often do we notice our surroundings?

This was not a strenuous activity because I practiced it frequently. I’m pretty familiar with the trails leading away from the university because it is my place to go to “get away from it all”. I’m too tired and frustrated to see the solution to a problem I am working on; I like to step away from it for a while and do something else. I once heard that if you ask your brain a question, it has no choice but to answer it (sometimes, it just takes a while). Even when consciously thinking of other things, your subconscious is still trying to solve the problem.

The first time I took to these trails to clear my head was nearly two years. I had a particularly heinous set of data from a lab, so I went to my instructor for help. Completely baffled by my results, he wasn’t sure if there was anything I could do because “you can’t make a silk purse out of a sow’s ear”. How was I supposed to complete my lab? I was already discouraged but then devastated. It was the dead of winter, but I needed to get away from the university, so I just started walking. I trudged through the snow until my cheeks were red, and my eyelashes froze. At first, I was trying to sort through the problem, but something about frozen eyelashes gives you a real perspective on life. Feeling greatly refreshed, I returned to work and eventually figured out several scenarios which could have caused the bad data (which is almost as good as good data).

As I found my point for my 40 minutes of “stillness”, I started by focusing on the sounds of my surroundings: the waves of traffic in the distance, geese flying overhead, rain drops hitting the lake. Eventually, I noticed some ducks in the distance and how they were resting on the lake with no waves. No waves seem a little puzzling on such a windy day. My mind wandered to the reasons why there were no waves. Is there something below the surface? Is it the result of destructive wave interference?

As we debriefed our activity, our instructor gave us some tips on using this activity with students. She said, “Even Grade 5 boys can learn to be still for 15 minutes and learn to appreciate it.” This got me thinking: how often do students get to practice being still? I don’t mean sitting at their desks all day, but how many students can sit and be quiet with no distractions? This is more important than ever in our constantly on-the-go society.
